The cylinder-to-liquid density ratio is \(\gamma=0.70\). The cylinder bottom is a few centimetres above the beaker bottom. The cylinder oscillates vertically, its axis always coinciding with the beaker axis. The liquid-level oscillation amplitude is \(A=1\,\mathrm{mm}\).
Find the period \(T\). Neglect the liquid viscosity.

statement.text:
T1: Floating cylinder
A solid uniform cylinder of height \(h=10\,\mathrm{cm}\) and base area \(s=100\,\mathrm{cm^2}\) floats in a cylindrical beaker of height \(H=20\,\mathrm{cm}\) and inner bottom area \(S=102\,\mathrm{cm^2}\), filled with liquid. The cylinder-to-liquid density ratio is \(\gamma=0.70\). The cylinder bottom is a few centimetres above the beaker bottom. The cylinder oscillates vertically, its axis always coinciding with the beaker axis. The liquid-level oscillation amplitude is \(A=1\,\mathrm{mm}\).
Find the period \(T\). Neglect the liquid viscosity.

children.text: Moving liquid volume \(sx_1\) from below the cylinder into the upper gap raises its centre by \(\gamma h+(x_1+x_2)/2\). Combine this with the cylinder's gravitational-energy loss:
\[U=-\gamma\rho shg x_1+\rho s x_1g\left(\gamma h+\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)=\frac12\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s}x_1^2.\]

The gap speed is \(s/(S-s)=50\) times the cylinder speed. Liquid below the cylinder has speed of the cylinder's order, so its kinetic energy is negligible compared with the fast annular flow. The small amplitude also allows the annular column height to be replaced by \(\gamma h\). Including both the cylinder and gap liquid gives
\[k_{\rm eff}=\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad m_{\rm eff}=\rho\gamma h\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\gamma h}{g}}\simeq0.53\,\mathrm s.\]
Ignoring the liquid inertia would produce a much shorter, incorrect period. The result uses the narrow-gap and small-amplitude approximations justified by the supplied dimensions.

nodes.alt: Original dynamical cross-sections with upward cylinder acceleration a1, downward annular-liquid acceleration a2, atmospheric pressure p0 at the free surface and pressure p below the cylinder.

children.text: Let the displaced cylinder accelerate upwards at \(a_1\), while the gap liquid accelerates downwards at \(a_2\). Continuity gives \(s a_1=(S-s)a_2\). Applying Newton's law to a unit-area liquid column of height \(l=\gamma h+x_1+x_2\), and to the cylinder, gives
\[p_0-p+\rho gl=\rho l a_2,\qquad (p-p_0)s-\gamma\rho shg=\gamma\rho sh a_1.\]

Eliminate \(p\) and neglect products of small displacements and accelerations. Then \(\rho gs(x_1+x_2)=\gamma\rho sh(a_1+a_2)\). Continuity reduces this to \(a_1=gx_1/(\gamma h)\), opposite to the displacement. It is the same harmonic motion. Pressure is approximately uniform under the cylinder because horizontal liquid accelerations there are much smaller than those in the gap. Both original marking schemes remain in the reference PDF.

solution.text:
T1: Floating cylinder
Solution I: energy
Let liquid density be \(\rho\). The equilibrium immersion depth is \(\gamma h\). If the cylinder moves down by \(x_1\) at speed \(v_1\), liquid in the narrow annular gap moves up by \(x_2\) at speed \(v_2\). Incompressibility gives
\[s x_1=(S-s)x_2,\qquad s v_1=(S-s)v_2.\]

Moving liquid volume \(sx_1\) from below the cylinder into the upper gap raises its centre by \(\gamma h+(x_1+x_2)/2\). Combine this with the cylinder's gravitational-energy loss:
\[U=-\gamma\rho shg x_1+\rho s x_1g\left(\gamma h+\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\right)=\frac12\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s}x_1^2.\]
The gap speed is \(s/(S-s)=50\) times the cylinder speed. Liquid below the cylinder has speed of the cylinder's order, so its kinetic energy is negligible compared with the fast annular flow. The small amplitude also allows the annular column height to be replaced by \(\gamma h\). Including both the cylinder and gap liquid gives
\[K=\frac12\gamma\rho shv_1^2+\frac12\rho(S-s)\gamma h v_2^2=\frac12\rho\gamma h\frac{sS}{S-s}v_1^2.\]
\[k_{\rm eff}=\rho g\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad m_{\rm eff}=\rho\gamma h\frac{sS}{S-s},\qquad T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\gamma h}{g}}\simeq0.53\,\mathrm s.\]
Ignoring the liquid inertia would produce a much shorter, incorrect period. The result uses the narrow-gap and small-amplitude approximations justified by the supplied dimensions.
Solution II: dynamics

Let the displaced cylinder accelerate upwards at \(a_1\), while the gap liquid accelerates downwards at \(a_2\). Continuity gives \(s a_1=(S-s)a_2\). Applying Newton's law to a unit-area liquid column of height \(l=\gamma h+x_1+x_2\), and to the cylinder, gives
\[p_0-p+\rho gl=\rho l a_2,\qquad (p-p_0)s-\gamma\rho shg=\gamma\rho sh a_1.\]
Eliminate \(p\) and neglect products of small displacements and accelerations. Then \(\rho gs(x_1+x_2)=\gamma\rho sh(a_1+a_2)\). Continuity reduces this to \(a_1=gx_1/(\gamma h)\), opposite to the displacement. It is the same harmonic motion. Pressure is approximately uniform under the cylinder because horizontal liquid accelerations there are much smaller than those in the gap. Both original marking schemes remain in the reference PDF.
